title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models

paper.title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive inference by leveraging the memory bound nature of decoding, verifying multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass.
For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation.
We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B–1T parameters, 8–512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size.
We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics.
At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts.
Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions.
We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative
Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sparse MoE architectures are increasingly used in high-capacity LLMs because they scale model capacity without proportionally increasing per-token compute [ 24 , 11 , 55 , 16 ] . At the same time, long-horizon agentic workloads, test-time scaling, RL rollouts with long-tailed completions, and smaller memory budgets increasingly push inference into low-batch regimes where token latency matters most [ 29 , 42 , 26 , 48 , 46 , 12 , 27 , 14 ] . Speculative decoding (SD) is a lossless way to reduce autoregressive latency: a draft model proposes K K tokens, and the target model evaluates the corresponding K + 1 K{+}1 positions in a single forward pass, amortizing the cost of a target-model invocation across positions [ 31 , 5 ] . Prior work suggests that SD is less effective for sparse MoE targets in this regime because verification may activate many additional experts and erode the expected gains [ 23 , 35 , 43 ] . For a fixed draft model, SD speedup is governed by the acceptance length and the verification cost. Most prior work focuses on improving acceptance length [ 35 , 36 , 4 ] , while verification cost is often treated as a simple function of architecture and batch size [ 42 ] . For sparse MoEs, however, verification cost depends on how many unique experts are activated across the B ⁡ ( K + 1 ) B(K{+}1) verification positions. MoESD [ 23 ] models this cost under an activated-expert-bytes view: in a memory-bandwidth-bound regime [ 52 ] , cost scales with the total expert-weight bytes loaded during verification, approximated as the unique-expert count multiplied by the per-expert byte size. For the MoE models studied there, this view aligns with the expected concave speedup curve and limited low-batch gains. We ask whether that conclusion continues to hold for recent fine-grained sparse MoE models on modern hardware, and evaluate it across 10 models spanning 30B–1T parameters and 8–512 experts. For each model, we use the supported SD mechanism (EAGLE, EAGLE-3, MTP, or a separate draft model; details in Appendix B ). Most of these models do not exhibit the predicted concave curve. Instead, many remain unusually efficient at low batch sizes and peak at or near batch size 1, precisely where the activated-expert-bytes view predicts limited SD gains for MoE targets. This discrepancy points to two mechanisms missing from the activated-expert-bytes view: 1. Temporal overlap in MoE routing across verification positions. In fine-grained MoE models [ 8 , 37 ] , adjacent positions share 20–45% of their activated experts, far above the 4–12% predicted by an independence baseline (which assumes experts are selected independently across positions given routing probabilities). This temporal overlap reduces the unique expert count during K + 1 K{+}1 -position verification by 21–34% relative to the independence baseline, and accounts for most of the overlap beyond the uniform baseline (which assumes experts are chosen uniformly at random across the expert pool; 69–92%) in high-sparsity models. 2. GPU execution dynamics. The activated-expert-bytes view ignores hardware-level effects that decouple parameter size from runtime, including memory hierarchy behavior (e.g., L2 cache reuse), kernel efficiency, and achieved FLOPs/bandwidth. For example, at batch size 1, activated-expert bytes are a poor proxy for latency: for Qwen3-30B FP8 on H100, MoE kernels reach 45–49% of peak HBM bandwidth while attention kernels reach only 22–25%, so MoE layers account for only 33% of forward-pass time despite representing 67% of model weights. When co-routed positions re-read the same small expert shard, L2 serves the repeated reads: in the same setting, the MoE L2 hit rate rises from 5.72% in AR decoding to 27.79% under SD verification. The low MoE runtime share also holds on B200 (35%), although the L2 hit rate there does not rise under SD: the specific mechanisms depend on the hardware and kernel, but the failure of activated-expert bytes as a cost proxy persists. Taken together, these results show that SD performance in sparse MoE models is governed not only by activated-expert bytes , but also by temporal routing overlap and GPU execution dynamics. This predictive capability is useful in practice because evaluating SD-relevant target and draft architecture choices by direct training-and-benchmarking is expensive, especially at frontier scales. We therefore introduce a maximum-entropy framework based on Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) that uses empirical pairwise overlap statistics to predict unique expert counts within 4% error and reproduce observed speedup curves under synthetic routing. The same framework enables train-free screening of target and draft design tradeoffs before full training, including sparser targets and MoE-versus-dense draft models.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • We provide a comprehensive empirical study of SD on 10 sparse MoE models spanning 30B–1T parameters and 8–512 experts, and show that fine-grained MoEs remain unusually efficient at low batch sizes and might even peak near batch size 1, contrary to the concave-curve prediction of the activated-expert-bytes view. • We quantify temporal routing overlap across draft positions, tasks, and languages, and show that consecutive positions in fine-grained MoE models reuse substantially more experts than an independent-routing baseline predicts. This overlap persists for rejected draft tokens and reduces the unique expert count during SD verification (§ 6 ). • We show that activated-expert bytes are a poor proxy for runtime at batch size 1 on both H100 and B200, and use detailed GPU profiling to identify the H100 mechanisms, HBM-bandwidth utilization gaps between MoE and attention kernels and L2 cache reuse for small expert shards, and to show that these mechanisms are kernel-dependent (§ 7 ). • We introduce a maximum-entropy IPF framework that predicts unique expert counts within 4% error and generates realistic token-to-expert assignments. Synthetic-routing experiments reproduce the observed speedup curve, and the same framework enables train-free screening of target and draft architecture tradeoffs, including sparser targets and MoE-versus-dense draft layers, before additional training (§ 8 , Appendix M.3 ).

sections.heading: MoE architectures and routing locality.
sections.text: Sparse MoE architectures trace back to sparsely-gated MoE [ 44 ] and later scaling and routing designs such as GShard [ 30 ] , BASE Layers [ 32 ] , Switch Transformers [ 17 ] , GLaM [ 15 ] , and Expert Choice Routing [ 57 ] . More recent language-model variants increasingly use finer-grained and shared-expert designs [ 28 , 8 , 24 , 11 , 55 , 16 ] . Prior work [ 40 , 3 ] shows that expert co-activation is influenced by semantic and positional similarity, and ExpertFlow [ 20 ] exploits this locality for memory-constrained deployment. We build on this line of work by quantifying how temporal locality across consecutive draft tokens changes speculative-verification cost.

sections.heading: Speculative decoding.
sections.text: Early work [ 47 ] introduced a prefix-validation approach for parallel autoregressive decoding. Modern speculative decoding methods differ mainly in how they construct and verify proposals: draft-model and seq2seq variants [ 31 , 5 , 53 ] , retrieval- or tree-based proposals [ 21 , 49 , 38 , 50 ] , extra decoding heads and multi-token prediction [ 4 , 2 , 19 , 11 , 55 ] , and higher-capacity or parallel drafting variants [ 35 , 34 , 36 , 18 , 25 , 22 ] . Recent work has shown that SD can remain effective outside the traditional small-batch dense regime, but for different reasons. MagicDec [ 42 ] shows that in long-context serving, large batches can again favor SD because KV-cache traffic dominates verification cost. The closest prior work for MoE is MoESD [ 23 ] , which models verification under an activated-expert-bytes view and accordingly predicts concave speedup curves with limited gains at low batch sizes. Because memory constraints typically force batch size down as sequence length grows, this low-batch regime is increasingly relevant for the longer-context, long-tailed RL rollout, and agentic workloads emerging in practice. Our work revisits this question for modern sparse MoEs and identifies a distinct regime in which fine-grained MoEs remain effective even at low batch sizes: temporal routing overlap and GPU execution dynamics yield higher speedup than the activated-expert-bytes view predicts.

sections.heading: 3 Background and Experimental Setup
sections.text: Each SD iteration has two phases: (1) a draft model proposes K K tokens, and (2) the target model verifies these draft tokens together with the next-token continuation in a single pass over K + 1 K{+}1 positions. SD helps Time per output token (TPOT) only when the savings from fewer target-model calls exceed the overhead of verification—i.e., when acceptance is high and verification is cheap. In MoE models, this verification cost depends not only on model size but also on routing behavior, because verifying multiple tokens may activate overlapping sets of experts across the K + 1 K{+}1 positions. Because different SD mechanisms have different acceptance behavior, we isolate the target-side verification cost using target efficiency (TE) [ 23 ] , TE = T target AR / T target SD , \mathrm{TE}=T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{AR}}/T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{SD}}, where T target AR T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{AR}} denotes the latency of a single-token autoregressive (AR) decoding step on the target model and T target SD T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{SD}} denotes the latency of the target model’s verification pass over K + 1 K{+}1 positions in speculative decoding (SD). A higher TE indicates that the SD verification pass is closer in cost to a standard AR decoding step. Because TE is independent of acceptance length, it lets us compare target-side verification efficiency across draft mechanisms and model architectures. The 10 evaluated MoE models span sparsity ratios (k/N, top-k over total experts) from 0.25 (Mixtral) to 0.020 (Qwen3-Next-80B), and per-expert weights from 4.7 MB to 176 MB in FP8, a 37× range that proves critical for GPU execution dynamics (§ 5 ); Appendix Table 6 lists the full architectural details and SD methods. All experiments use K = 3 K{=}3 draft tokens, vLLM v1 (commit 7c080dd3c ) [ 29 ] , and MT-Bench [ 56 ] as the base dataset; Appendix B provides details on the sweep schedule, token output lengths, and disabled prefix caching, Section 9.1 and Section 9.2 evaluate larger K K and long-context serving, and Appendix A discusses the remaining scope of the K K and hardware assumptions. All models run on NVIDIA H100 SXM GPUs except for Kimi-K2.5 and DeepSeek-V3 which use NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

sections.heading: 4 Speedup Curve Regimes
sections.text: Figure 1 : TPOT speedup versus batch size for four representative MoE models. Mixtral-8x7B exhibits the predicted concave curve, whereas the other three are non-concave and peak at or near batch size 1. We begin by characterizing the observed speedup regimes. Figure 1 shows TPOT speedup ( TPOT vanilla / TPOT sd \text{TPOT}_{\text{vanilla}}/\text{TPOT}_{\text{sd}} ) versus batch size for four representative models, where TPOT denotes wall-clock time per output token. Appendix C shows all the 10-grid. MoESD [ 23 ] predicts a concave speedup curve that peaks at intermediate batch sizes, where expert activation saturates. Under this view, speedup at low batch sizes remains limited because verification must load additional experts. We observe a concave pattern in less sparse MoEs with larger per-expert weights (e.g., Qwen2-57B, Mixtral-8x7B). In contrast, sparser models with smaller experts (e.g., Qwen3-235B, Kimi-K2.5) exhibit non-concave curves, often peaking at batch size 1. The non-concave behavior is also not specific to MT-Bench: Appendix D shows that Qwen3-30B and Qwen3-235B retain qualitatively similar speedup curves across multiple datasets (Figure 7 ). We find that the speedup-curve shape closely tracks target efficiency at batch size 1, which measures how expensive it is for the target model to verify K + 1 K{+}1 tokens instead of decoding a single token. Lower target efficiency leaves more headroom for the classic concave rise, whereas higher target efficiency leads to non-concave behavior, as shown in Figure 6 . Qwen3.5-35B (bf16, TP2) is a notable exception: it exhibits non-concave behavior despite having lower target efficiency than GLM-4.7-Flash (bf16, TP1). Table 1 reports the measured target efficiency for the main-text configurations alongside the activated-expert-bytes prediction; Appendix Table 10 reports the full cross-model measurements across SD methods, TP settings, and precisions. We find that target efficiency varies substantially even within a single model family as we change SD method, TP, and precision. In general, increasing TP or using lower precision increases target efficiency at batch size 1 and shift peak speedup toward smaller batch sizes. We analyze these effects in more detail in § 5 .

sections.heading: 5 Limits of the Activated-Expert-Bytes View
sections.text: At low batch size ∼ \sim 1, decoding processes a single token per sequence, making the linear layers largely memory-bandwidth-bound in the roofline sense [ 52 ] : execution time is therefore dominated by loading weights from HBM rather than by compute. A first-principles estimate therefore assumes GPU time is proportional to weight bytes: Target efficiency ≈ C dense + k ⋅ C expert C dense + unique sd ⋅ C expert , \text{Target efficiency}\;\approx\;\frac{C_{\text{dense}}+k\cdot C_{\text{expert}}}{C_{\text{dense}}+\text{unique}_{\text{sd}}\cdot C_{\text{expert}}}, (1) where C dense C_{\text{dense}} is the per-GPU dense weight bytes (attention + shared expert), C expert C_{\text{expert}} is the per-expert weight bytes, and unique sd \text{unique}_{\text{sd}} is the empirical unique expert count during SD verification. Even when using the empirical unique sd \text{unique}_{\text{sd}} measured from actual MT-Bench routing, this activated-expert-bytes model systematically underestimates target efficiency (Table 1 ). The gap ranges from + 0.06 +0.06 (Mixtral, large experts) to + 0.37 +0.37 (Qwen3-235B, small experts). Weight bytes alone do not explain the GPU execution time at batch size 1. This activated-expert-bytes estimate omits critical model behavior and hardware interactions which we will discuss in detail in the following sections. sections.heading: 6 Temporal Overlap in MoE Expert Routing

Independence baseline : uses the empirical per-layer expert probabilities { p e } \{p_{e}\} while assuming tokens are routed independently. This captures savings from non-uniform expert popularity. 3. Empirical : measured from consecutive tokens on a real dataset, preserving temporal overlap. We report routing-overlap statistics for the models in our SD setup; details in Appendix H . sections.heading: 6.1 Applicability to draft tokens.
sections.text: The overlap measurements above use accepted continuations. If rejected draft tokens were routed to substantially different experts, accepted-token overlap would mischaracterize the routing patterns encountered during SD verification. In aggregate MT-Bench, however, rejected tokens share a similar fraction of top- k k experts with the preceding token, and in some cases slightly more. The deconfounded accepted-vs.-first-rejection comparison in Appendix H shows the same pattern for Qwen3-235B at step 1, where first-rejection tokens have higher overlap than accepted tokens (0.488 vs. 0.447; Table 14 ). We therefore treat accepted-token overlap as a conservative proxy for aggregate verification cost.

sections.heading: 7 Interaction of GPU execution of sparse MoE on Speculative Decoding
sections.text: The preceding analysis shows that SD verification activates substantially fewer unique experts than an independence-based routing model would predict. However, temporal overlap alone does not fully explain the gap between activated-expert-bytes estimates and measured verification cost at batch size 1. The realized cost of loading experts also depends on how sparse MoE kernels execute on GPU hardware. We therefore turn to GPU execution dynamics, which govern how expert loading translates into observed latency through bandwidth utilization and cache behavior. We profile Qwen3-30B and Mixtral at batch size 1 on H100 using Nsight Systems (kernel timing) and Nsight Compute (hardware counters), and repeat the profiling for Qwen3-235B on H100 and for Qwen3-30B and Mixtral on B200 (Appendix F ). sections.heading: L2 cache reuse across co-routed experts.
sections.text: The activated-expert-bytes model assumes that MoE cost scales linearly with the number of unique experts loaded. At batch size 1, the default H100 MoE kernel processes each (token, expert) pair in its own thread block, so when multiple verification tokens are routed to the same small expert (Section 6 ), its weights are read once per token and the repeated reads are served from L2 rather than HBM. For Qwen3-30B, the L2 hit rate rises from 5.72% to 27.79% for 4.5 MB experts, whose working set partially fits within the H100’s 50 MB L2 cache. For Mixtral, the kernel groups co-routed tokens by expert under SD, so each expert is read once and there are no repeated reads to absorb (1.68% in both modes); its 168 MB experts would far exceed L2 in any case. Without L2, these repeated reads would make HBM traffic grow with the number of (token, expert) pairs rather than with the number of unique experts; L2 brings it back close to the unique-expert bytes that the activated-expert-bytes model assumes. The lower S MoE S_{\text{MoE}} of Qwen3-30B (1.57 vs. 2.19 for Mixtral, despite a similar 2.4–2.5 × \times unique-expert multiple; Section 6 ) therefore likely stems mainly from bandwidth utilization, discussed below.

sections.heading: Factors affecting L2 cache reuse.
sections.text: Table 1 shows that, within a model family, higher tensor parallelism and lower-precision weights tend to increase target efficiency. Qwen3-30B illustrates the effect concretely: target efficiency rises from 0.630 to 0.697 when TP increases from 1 to 2 at BF16, and from 0.630 to 0.818 when weights are quantized from BF16 to FP8 at TP1; the combined FP8, TP2 configuration reaches 0.860. One contributing mechanism is that tensor parallelism reduces the per-GPU expert shard size, while quantization further shrinks each shard, allowing more of the co-routed expert working set to stay in L2 between repeated reads. By contrast, Mixtral’s experts are so large that even a single expert does not fit in L2, so the scope for additional reuse is limited and the improvement remains small across the available EAGLE configurations. Appendix Figure 5 shows the corresponding Qwen3-30B configuration sweep.

sections.heading: HBM bandwidth utilization disparity.
sections.text: At batch size 1, FP8 attention GEMM kernels launch far fewer CTAs than FP8 MoE kernels, leaving many SMs idle and therefore achieving substantially lower HBM bandwidth (Table 5 ). This pattern is consistent with prior work on attention kernels, which emphasizes IO-aware scheduling and improved work partitioning [ 9 , 10 ] . As a result, MoE accounts for less GPU time than its weight share would suggest. For Qwen3-30B, the roughly 2 × \times bandwidth advantage of MoE GEMMs over attention GEMMs compresses the MoE contribution from 67% of weights to 33% of runtime. For Mixtral, MoE and attention GEMMs achieve more similar bandwidth, so the MoE runtime share remains closer to its weight share. Verifying K + 1 K{+}1 tokens barely increases attention cost ( S = 1.02 S{=}1.02 ) because KV-cache reads are reused across consecutive draft tokens, making MoE the principal source of SD slowdown in this regime. Consequently, the smaller MoE runtime share in Qwen3-30B makes SD verification faster than the activated-expert-bytes model would predict. For Mixtral, larger matrices enable more CTAs for attention, narrowing both the bandwidth gap and the activated-expert-bytes-model error.

sections.heading: Expert size as the unifying factor.
sections.text: On H100, both mechanisms are governed primarily by expert size. Large experts achieve high bandwidth utilization and exceed L2 capacity, so execution time remains approximately proportional to weight bytes and the activated-expert-bytes model is relatively accurate. Small experts leave bandwidth underutilized, making execution time substantially smaller than the activated-expert-bytes model would predict, while L2 absorbs repeated reads of co-routed experts. A full three-step correction chain that raises the estimate from 0.51 to 0.872 for Qwen3-30B is provided in Appendix E . Qwen3-235B (FP8, TP4) reproduces the same mechanisms on H100, with the largest weight-model gap among the profiled models (+0.38; Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 8 End-to-end validation via synthetic routing.
sections.text: Section 6 and Section 7 show that both temporal overlap and GPU execution dynamics shape the SD speedup curves of MoE models. We therefore conduct synthetic experiments that combine these two factors to predict the speedup curves without using trained weights. The only assumption is access to reasonable expert-overlap statistics, obtained either from a model in the same family or from the averages in Table 17 . To evaluate the IPF framework from Section 6.3 and its synthetic-routing construction from Appendix L , we replace the model’s learned routing with IPF-generated synthetic routing while keeping all other inference settings fixed (dummy weights, same hardware). Because this method runs the real kernels on the target hardware, it captures hardware- and kernel-specific execution effects, such as those that differ between H100 and B200, without modeling them explicitly. We define the proxy target efficiency as T vanilla proxy / T SD proxy T_{\text{vanilla}}^{\text{proxy}}/T_{\text{SD}}^{\text{proxy}} , where T vanilla proxy T_{\text{vanilla}}^{\text{proxy}} = forward pass + logits + sampling, and T SD proxy T_{\text{SD}}^{\text{proxy}} = forward pass + logits + rejection sampling + draft. We measure the proxy target efficiency under three routing assumptions: uniform random routing, uniform IPF routing with the same routing-overlap statistics in every MoE layer, and per-layer skewed IPF routing. Figure 2 compares these three settings. The uniform-random baseline consistently underestimates the target efficiency at small batch sizes, and the error is larger for sparser MoE models. Per-layer IPF synthetic routing closely tracks the real-model curves at small batch sizes and remains closer than uniform random routing across the full batch-size range. For Qwen3-30B (Figure 2 2(b) ), we show all three routing variants for comparison. Although the skewed IPF variant is more accurate, the uniform IPF variant still captures the qualitative batch-size trends of the real-model SD speedup curves. Residual gaps between the IPF-generated synthetic routing and the real-model curves are expected because the synthetic routing does not exactly reproduce the full routing distribution of the real model. In particular, higher-order statistics not captured by the pairwise routing-overlap constraints and position-independent per-expert marginals in Eq. 2 may still affect performance. Nevertheless, predicting these curves without training a model requires only uniform IPF together with routing-overlap statistics taken either from the same model family or from the averages in Table 17 . These results show that routing-overlap statistics captured by the IPF framework substantially reduce the gap between synthetic and real-model curves relative to the uniform-random baseline, while preserving the relevant hardware-execution dynamics. Our main experiments fix K = 3 K{=}3 , a common production setting [ 51 , 39 , 41 ] . To test whether the observed curve shapes depend on this choice, we repeat the end-to-end sweep at K ∈ { 3 , 5 , 7 } K\in\{3,5,7\} for one model from each regime: Mixtral-8x7B (FP8, TP1, EAGLE), Qwen3-30B (FP8, TP2, EAGLE-3), and Qwen3-235B (FP8, TP4, EAGLE-3), all on H100 with MT-Bench (Figure 3 ). For all three models, the curve family is the same at every K K : Qwen3-30B and Qwen3-235B remain non-concave and peak at batch size 1, whereas Mixtral remains concave, with its best speedup near batch size 16. Our curve taxonomy (§ 4 ) is therefore not an artifact of K = 3 K{=}3 .

sections.heading: 9.2 Long-Context Inference
sections.text: Our main sweeps use short MT-Bench prompts. To test the long-context regime, where KV-cache traffic becomes increasingly dominant, we repeat the end-to-end sweep for Qwen3-30B (FP8, TP2, EAGLE-3, K = 3 K{=}3 ) on the throughput_32k split of SPEED-Bench [ 1 ] , which has prompts of about 32k tokens, with 4096-token outputs (Figure 4 ). The KV cache limits the maximum batch size to 24. Target efficiency is higher than on MT-Bench at every batch size. This is consistent with KV-cache reads, which both vanilla decoding and SD verification incur, diluting the relative cost of the extra expert weights loaded during verification. The curve also remains non-concave: target efficiency is highest at batch size 1, dips at batch size 4, and recovers at larger batch sizes. Long context thus makes verification relatively cheaper for the MoE target; MagicDec [ 42 ] studies this regime in depth.

sections.heading: 9.3 Implications for MoE Draft Layers
sections.text: Current SD drafters commonly use a dense transformer layer. In Appendix M , we use the framework from Section 8 to analyze the effect of an MoE drafter when the target model is also an MoE model. The analysis suggests that MoE draft layers may become attractive in sufficiently sparse regimes. At low-to-medium batch sizes, an MoE drafter does not improve target efficiency, but if trained effectively it could still improve end-to-end speedup through longer acceptance lengths enabled by its additional parameters. At larger batch sizes, the MoE drafter becomes more attractive because it remains less compute-bound than a dense drafter when the target model itself is MoE. To probe a sparser setting than Qwen3-30B, we also simulate a 896-expert architecture (<1% activations) and show in Appendix M.3 that the MoE drafter becomes more favorable as the target model remains bandwidth-bound. Because this analysis is synthetic and does not measure acceptance-length gains from trained MoE drafters, we interpret it as a design study rather than direct evidence for trained MoE drafters.

sections.heading: 9.4 Routing Inertia in Rejected Draft Tokens
sections.text: Expert routing does not cleanly separate accepted from rejected draft tokens in a way that would support early termination. In the aggregate MT-Bench analysis, fine-grained models show comparable or slightly higher overlap for rejected tokens, and held-out Spec-Bench and Aya [ 45 ] slices preserve the same tendency in median, with some task- and language-specific reversals (Appendix H.8 ). Even in the largest stable aggregate effect (Qwen3-235B, Cohen’s d ≈ − 0.3 d\approx-0.3 ), the accepted and rejected distributions still overlap by ∼ 85 % {\sim}85\% , and most held-out slices remain negligible or small in effect size. These results suggest that routing-based rejection predictors are unlikely to be useful in practice: routing inertia is statistically robust but offers limited leverage for early-exit decisions.

sections.heading: 10 Conclusion
sections.text: As sparse MoE models move into increasingly memory-constrained inference regimes, an important question is whether speculative decoding remains worthwhile at low batch size. Across 10 recent sparse MoE models (30B–1T parameters, 8–512 experts), we find that the previously expected concave SD speedup curve does not characterize most modern sparse models: many attain high speedup at or near batch size 1. We show that verification cost in sparse MoE models is not determined by activated-expert bytes alone, but is also shaped by temporal overlap across consecutive tokens and by GPU execution dynamics, whose specific mechanisms vary across hardware and kernels. A maximum-entropy IPF framework predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4% error and, under synthetic routing with fixed execution conditions, substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves while capturing the qualitative low-batch trend, thereby providing a train-free way to study target and draft architecture tradeoffs. Taken together, these results suggest that SD performance on sparse MoE models should be modeled using both routing-overlap statistics and GPU execution dynamics, and that fine-grained MoE designs may be more compatible with low-batch speculative inference than previously believed.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations
sections.text: Our synthetic-routing analysis is approximate. The IPF construction matches pairwise overlap statistics, but does not model higher-order routing structure, position dependence in expert marginals, or how temporal overlap itself varies with architectural choices. In practice, one may use overlap statistics from a closely related model family, or aggregate statistics from the models we study, as a better train-free estimate than a uniform baseline when exploring target and draft design tradeoffs before training. However, understanding which architectural factors determine temporal overlap, and how reliably overlap transfers across model families and sparsity patterns, remains an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix F Additional GPU Profiling: Qwen3-235B and B200
sections.text: Table 12 extends the H100 profiling of Table 5 to a second fine-grained model on H100 (Qwen3-235B, FP8, TP4) and to Qwen3-30B and Mixtral on B200 (FP8, TP1), using the same Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute methodology at batch size 1. Each configuration uses the MoE kernel that vLLM selects by default. The main result is that the activated-expert-bytes model fails as a cost model for sparse MoE verification in every configuration we profile : it underpredicts target efficiency by 0.18–0.38 across all three configurations in Table 12 , in addition to the H100 gaps of Table 5 , and the error is largest for fine-grained models with small experts. The mechanisms behind the error differ across hardware and kernels, but the error itself persists. Qwen3-235B reproduces both H100 mechanisms: MoE kernels achieve higher bandwidth than attention kernels, and the L2 hit rate rises under SD.

sections.heading: B200.
sections.text: On B200, the phenomenon reproduces: MoE accounts for 35% and 69% of GPU time for Qwen3-30B and Mixtral (vs. 33% and 75% on H100), and the activated-expert-bytes model still underpredicts target efficiency (0.76 and 0.61 observed vs. 0.51 and 0.43 predicted), with the larger gap again for the smaller experts. The H100 mechanisms, however, do not carry over. The default MoE kernel for Qwen3-30B on B200 groups co-routed tokens by expert and reads each expert’s weights once, so there are no repeated reads for L2 to absorb and the L2 hit rate does not rise under SD (2.49% → \to 2.21%); attention and MoE kernels both run at only 12–15% of peak bandwidth, leaving no attention-vs.-MoE disparity. The L2 hit rate thus reflects kernel design rather than hardware: running the default H100 MoE kernel on B200 with the same IPF routing gives an SD L2 hit rate of 27.19% for Qwen3-30B FP8, close to the 27.79% measured on H100. This suggests that at batch size 1 on B200, step time is dominated by costs that do not scale with expert bytes, likely fixed per-step overheads. The common principle is that runtime depends on the bandwidth each kernel achieves and on fixed per-step costs, whereas the activated-expert-bytes model assumes weight bytes at a single constant bandwidth: on H100 achieved bandwidth differs sharply between kernels, and on B200 fixed costs dominate. Verification cost should therefore be measured on the target hardware rather than derived from weight bytes, which is what the synthetic-routing method in Section 8 does. sections.heading: Appendix H Routing Inertia in Rejected Draft Tokens
sections.text: Section 6.2 showed that, in the aggregate MT-Bench analysis, rejected draft tokens in fine-grained models exhibit equal or higher expert overlap than accepted tokens, supporting the sub-linear verification-cost argument for SD. Here we present the full statistical analysis underlying that claim and summarize the held-out Spec-Bench and Aya results.

sections.heading: H.1 Methodology
sections.text: We record per-token expert assignments for every verification step during SD inference with an EAGLE draft model and K = 3 K{=}3 . Because vLLM’s enable_return_routed_experts API returns routed experts only for accepted tokens by default, we extended the instrumentation to record routed experts for rejected tokens as well. Each step j ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } j\in\{1,2,3\} is labeled as accepted or rejected by the target model. For every pair of steps ( j − 1 , j ) (j{-}1,j) , we compute the consecutive overlap ratio : the fraction of top- k k experts shared between them. A naive accepted-versus-rejected comparison conflates two distinct populations: when step j j is accepted, step j − 1 j{-}1 is always accepted, whereas when step j j is rejected, step j − 1 j{-}1 may be either accepted or rejected. We resolve this confound with a three-way partition : • Accepted : step j j accepted, step j − 1 j{-}1 accepted (normal pair). • First-rejection : step j j rejected, step j − 1 j{-}1 accepted (clean comparison). • Cascade : step j j rejected, step j − 1 j{-}1 rejected (successive rejection). The accepted vs. first-rejection comparison is the cleanest test: both populations have an accepted predecessor, isolating the effect of token correctness on expert routing.

sections.heading: Appendix L Synthetic Routing Generation via IPF
sections.text: The IPF framework described in § 6.3 models each expert’s activation across B = 4 B{=}4 consecutive tokens as a set of correlated binary variables X 1 , … , X 4 ∈ { 0 , 1 } X_{1},\ldots,X_{4}\in\{0,1\} . The constraints are: • Marginals : P e ​ ( X t = 1 ) = p e P_{e}(X_{t}{=}1)=p_{e} (per-expert probability, or k / N k/N in the uniform variant). • Pairwise joints : P e ​ ( X t = 1 ∧ X t + j = 1 ) = overlap j × p e P_{e}(X_{t}{=}1\wedge X_{t+j}{=}1)=\text{overlap}_{j}\times p_{e} for steps j = 1 , 2 , 3 j{=}1,2,3 . IPF iteratively rescales the distribution over the 2 4 = 16 2^{4}{=}16 states to satisfy all four marginal and six pairwise constraints. The predicted unique expert count is ∑ e [ 1 − P e ​ ( X 1 = 0 , … , X 4 = 0 ) ] \sum_{e}[1-P_{e}(X_{1}{=}0,\ldots,X_{4}{=}0)] , where P e P_{e} denotes the fitted joint distribution for expert e e .

sections.heading: Uniform vs. skewed variants.
sections.text: The uniform variant uses a single marginal p = k / N p{=}k/N for all experts and a single IPF solve. The skewed variant bins experts by their empirical probability (20 bins per layer), solves a separate IPF problem for each bin, and sums the per-expert contributions. The skewed variant captures both temporal overlap and non-uniform expert popularity, reducing the maximum prediction error from + 4.7 % +4.7\% (uniform IPF, under 5%) to + 3.7 % +3.7\% (skewed IPF, under 4%).

sections.heading: Synthetic routing generation.
sections.text: Beyond prediction, the same framework can generate synthetic token-to-expert assignments: (1) sample N N independent 4-bit patterns from the IPF distribution and (2) repair cardinality to enforce exactly k k active experts per token via single-expert swaps that minimize overlap error. In the skewed mode, the resulting per-layer expert probabilities are matched, achieving r > 0.99 r{>}0.99 correlation with the real routing distributions. These assignments are used in the dummy-weight experiment (§ 6.3 , Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: Appendix M MoE Draft Layer Analysis
sections.text: Section 9.3 raised the possibility that MoE draft layers may become attractive in sufficiently sparse regimes. This appendix addresses a narrower question: under the routing and hardware conditions of the measured models, when would an MoE drafter become cheaper than the dense drafters used in current SD systems?

sections.heading: M.1 Analytical Cost Model
sections.text: Current SD drafters such as EAGLE-3 and MTP use a dense transformer layer. For Qwen3-30B, a one-layer MoE drafter has the same effective width as the dense drafter ( top-k × expert intermediate = dense intermediate = 6144 \text{top-k}\times\text{expert intermediate}=\text{dense intermediate}=6144 ), and therefore approximately the same per-step cost at batch size 1, while exposing all N = 128 N{=}128 expert weight matrices. If training could exploit this additional capacity, it might improve acceptance length without increasing draft latency; however, we do not train such drafters here and treat this only as a synthetic design study. For an L L -layer MoE target with dense intermediate d dense = k × d expert d_{\text{dense}}=k\times d_{\text{expert}} , a single MoE draft layer has the same effective width as a dense layer at batch size 1. We predict the MoE draft cost at batch size b b by anchoring at batch size 1 and adding the measured incremental per-layer cost: T moe_drafter ​ ( b ) = T dense_drafter ​ ( 1 ) + T moe_target_AR ​ ( b ) − T moe_target_AR ​ ( 1 ) L , T_{\text{moe\_drafter}}(b)=T_{\text{dense\_drafter}}(1)+\frac{T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(b)-T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(1)}{L}, (11) where T moe_target_AR ​ ( b ) T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(b) is the measured AR forward-pass time at batch size b b . T dense_drafter ​ ( 1 ) T_{\text{dense\_drafter}}(1) captures any fixed framework overhead. T moe_target_AR ​ ( b ) − T moe_target_AR ​ ( 1 ) L \frac{T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(b)-T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(1)}{L} captures the incremental per-layer MoE cost. Naively using T moe_target_AR ​ ( b ) − T moe_target_AR ​ ( 1 ) L \frac{T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(b)-T_{\text{moe\_target\_AR}}(1)}{L} as the drafter cost would underestimate the true cost, because some layerwise latency is hidden when multiple layers execute in a pipelined stack but becomes exposed when only a single layer is used. This anchoring avoids double-counting attention costs while capturing both the transition from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound regimes and any fixed framework overhead.

sections.heading: M.2 Target Efficiency and Draft Cost for Qwen3-30B
sections.text: Figure 11 shows the measured target efficiency of a dense draft layer and a synthetic MoE draft layer, together with the prediction from Equation 11 . Figure 11 11(b) shows that the MoE drafter is slower at small batch sizes, but the dense drafter becomes compute-bound earlier and becomes more expensive at larger batch sizes. This behavior is consistent with the lower arithmetic intensity of MoE layers relative to dense layers [ 23 ] . Because the target model also contains MoE layers, its scaling remains closer to that of an MoE drafter than to that of a dense drafter. As a result, the dense drafter yields lower target efficiency at larger batch sizes, making the MoE drafter more attractive in that regime. This gap widens further for multi-layer drafters, which are increasingly common in recent SD work [ 25 ] . (a) Target efficiency (b) Total draft time (all K K steps). Figure 11 : Dense draft cost for Qwen3-30B ( L = 48 L{=}48 , N = 128 N{=}128 ). The dense drafter becomes more expensive at large batch sizes. With one layer, the MoE drafter has only a modest effect on target efficiency, but if trained effectively it could still improve end-to-end speedup by increasing acceptance length through its additional parameters. The gap magnifies for multi-layer drafts (e.g., five layers): the total cost of five dense layers grows superlinearly at high batch sizes, whereas five MoE layers would track the target’s scaling more closely.

sections.heading: M.3 Synthetic Experiment with N = 896 N{=}896
sections.text: For Qwen3-30B with N = 128 N{=}128 experts, the MoE drafter’s advantage over the dense drafter appears only at very large batch sizes, beyond the regime where SD is most effective. To test whether this advantage broadens in sparser architectures, we extrapolate to N = 896 N{=}896 experts (keeping k = 8 k{=}8 , d expert = 768 d_{\text{expert}}{=}768 ) using dummy weights and uniform IPF routing with the overlap statistics from Qwen3-30B ( N = 128 N{=}128 ) in every layer. Figure 12 shows the results. With N = 896 N{=}896 , the MoE draft layer remains bandwidth-bound to much larger batch sizes, consistent with prior analysis [ 23 ] . Even at moderate to large batch sizes, the MoE drafter has a similar effect on the speedup curve as the dense drafter, unlike the N = 128 N{=}128 case where the MoE advantage, assuming the same acceptance length, emerges only at very large batch sizes. The target-efficiency benefit is correspondingly more pronounced for larger number of layers, consistent with the trend in the N = 128 N{=}128 setting. These synthetic results suggest that MoE draft layers may become attractive over a broader batch-size range in sufficiently sparse architectures. (a) Draft / forward ratio ( N = 896 N{=}896 ). (b) Total draft time ( N = 896 N{=}896 ). Figure 12 : Synthetic MoE draft analysis for N = 896 N{=}896 (extrapolated from Qwen3-30B with dummy weights). The MoE layer remains bandwidth-bound to larger batch sizes, keeping the draft ratio flat where the dense drafter’s ratio rises.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: The checklist is designed to encourage best practices for responsible machine learning research, addressing issues of reproducibility, transparency, research ethics, and societal impact. Do not remove the checklist: The papers not including the checklist will be desk rejected. The checklist should follow the references and follow the (optional) supplemental material. The checklist does NOT count towards the page limit. Please read the checklist guidelines carefully for information on how to answer these questions. For each question in the checklist: • You should answer [Yes] , [No] , or [N/A] . • [N/A] means either that the question is Not Applicable for that particular paper or the relevant information is Not Available. • Please provide a short (1–2 sentence) justification right after your answer (even for [N/A] ). The checklist answers are an integral part of your paper submission. They are visible to the reviewers, area chairs, senior area chairs, and ethics reviewers. You will also be asked to include it (after eventual revisions) with the final version of your paper, and its final version will be published with the paper. The reviewers of your paper will be asked to use the checklist as one of the factors in their evaluation. While [Yes] is generally preferable to [No] , it is perfectly acceptable to answer [No] provided a proper justification is given (e.g., error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive” or “we were unable to find the license for the dataset we used”). In general, answering [No] or [N/A] is not grounds for rejection. While the questions are phrased in a binary way, we acknowledge that the true answer is often more nuanced, so please just use your best judgment and write a justification to elaborate. All supporting evidence can appear either in the main paper or the supplemental material, provided in appendix. If you answer [Yes] to a question, in the justification please point to the section(s) where related material for the question can be found. IMPORTANT, please: • Delete this instruction block, but keep the section heading “NeurIPS Paper Checklist" , • Keep the checklist subsection headings, questions/answers and guidelines below. • Do not modify the questions and only use the provided macros for your answers . 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The claims made in abstract and introduction are theoretically motivated and experimentally validated in Sections 4 , 6 , 7 , 8 , and M.3 . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper discusses the limitations of the work in Section A . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Please refer to Section 6.3 and Appendix G and L for the full set of assumptions and proofs. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We disclose our experimental setup needed to reproduce results in Appendix B . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We disclose our experimental setup in Appendix B . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Every end-to-end speedup measurement was repeated over 3 runs in independent server sessions, and the coefficient of variation (std/mean) of the speedup is below 5% at every batch size for every configuration (Appendix B ). Within each run, output token latency is measured as the median over 20k–655k output tokens during the benchmark client run. We also repeat the measurement for speedup curve on different datasets (MT-Bench, ShareGPT, InstructCoder, SpecBench (13 categories)) to ensure robustness in Figure 7 . We also repeat the measurement of difference in temporal overlap between accepted and rejected hypotheses in Appendix H.8 on SpecBench (13 categories) and Aya (7 languages) to ensure robustness beyond MT-Bench. We report standard error and Cohen’s d for the difference in temporal overlap between accepted and rejected hypotheses in Appendix H to quantify the statistical significance of the difference. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation. We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B–1T parameters, 8–512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size. We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics. At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts. Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions. We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing. 1 Introduction Sparse MoE architectures are increasingly used in high-capacity LLMs because they scale model capacity without proportionally increasing per-token compute [ 24 , 11 , 55 , 16 ] . At the same time, long-horizon agentic workloads, test-time scaling, RL rollouts with long-tailed completions, and smaller memory budgets increasingly push inference into low-batch regimes where token latency matters most [ 29 , 42 , 26 , 48 , 46 , 12 , 27 , 14 ] . Speculative decoding (SD) is a lossless way to reduce autoregressive latency: a draft model proposes K K tokens, and the target model evaluates the corresponding K + 1 K{+}1 positions in a single forward pass, amortizing the cost of a target-model invocation across positions [ 31 , 5 ] . Prior work suggests that SD is less effective for sparse MoE targets in this regime because verification may activate many additional experts and erode the expected gains [ 23 , 35 , 43 ] . For a fixed draft model, SD speedup is governed by the acceptance length and the verification cost. Most prior work focuses on improving acceptance length [ 35 , 36 , 4 ] , while verification cost is often treated as a simple function of architecture and batch size [ 42 ] . For sparse MoEs, however, verification cost depends on how many unique experts are activated across the B ⁡ ( K + 1 ) B(K{+}1) verification positions. MoESD [ 23 ] models this cost under an activated-expert-bytes view: in a memory-bandwidth-bound regime [ 52 ] , cost scales with the total expert-weight bytes loaded during verification, approximated as the unique-expert count multiplied by the per-expert byte size. For the MoE models studied there, this view aligns with the expected concave speedup curve and limited low-batch gains. We ask whether that conclusion continues to hold for recent fine-grained sparse MoE models on modern hardware, and evaluate it across 10 models spanning 30B–1T parameters and 8–512 experts. For each model, we use the supported SD mechanism (EAGLE, EAGLE-3, MTP, or a separate draft model; details in Appendix B ). Most of these models do not exhibit the predicted concave curve. Instead, many remain unusually efficient at low batch sizes and peak at or near batch size 1, precisely where the activated-expert-bytes view predicts limited SD gains for MoE targets. This discrepancy points to two mechanisms missing from the activated-expert-bytes view: 1. Temporal overlap in MoE routing across verification positions. In fine-grained MoE models [ 8 , 37 ] , adjacent positions share 20–45% of their activated experts, far above the 4–12% predicted by an independence baseline (which assumes experts are selected independently across positions given routing probabilities). This temporal overlap reduces the unique expert count during K + 1 K{+}1 -position verification by 21–34% relative to the independence baseline, and accounts for most of the overlap beyond the uniform baseline (which assumes experts are chosen uniformly at random across the expert pool; 69–92%) in high-sparsity models. 2. GPU execution dynamics. The activated-expert-bytes view ignores hardware-level effects that decouple parameter size from runtime, including memory hierarchy behavior (e.g., L2 cache reuse), kernel efficiency, and achieved FLOPs/bandwidth. For example, at batch size 1, activated-expert bytes are a poor proxy for latency: for Qwen3-30B FP8 on H100, MoE kernels reach 45–49% of peak HBM bandwidth while attention kernels reach only 22–25%, so MoE layers account for only 33% of forward-pass time despite representing 67% of model weights. When co-routed positions re-read the same small expert shard, L2 serves the repeated reads: in the same setting, the MoE L2 hit rate rises from 5.72% in AR decoding to 27.79% under SD verification. The low MoE runtime share also holds on B200 (35%), although the L2 hit rate there does not rise under SD: the specific mechanisms depend on the hardware and kernel, but the failure of activated-expert bytes as a cost proxy persists. Taken together, these results show that SD performance in sparse MoE models is governed not only by activated-expert bytes , but also by temporal routing overlap and GPU execution dynamics. This predictive capability is useful in practice because evaluating SD-relevant target and draft architecture choices by direct training-and-benchmarking is expensive, especially at frontier scales. We therefore introduce a maximum-entropy framework based on Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) that uses empirical pairwise overlap statistics to predict unique expert counts within 4% error and reproduce observed speedup curves under synthetic routing. The same framework enables train-free screening of target and draft design tradeoffs before full training, including sparser targets and MoE-versus-dense draft models. Contributions. • We provide a comprehensive empirical study of SD on 10 sparse MoE models spanning 30B–1T parameters and 8–512 experts, and show that fine-grained MoEs remain unusually efficient at low batch sizes and might even peak near batch size 1, contrary to the concave-curve prediction of the activated-expert-bytes view. • We quantify temporal routing overlap across draft positions, tasks, and languages, and show that consecutive positions in fine-grained MoE models reuse substantially more experts than an independent-routing baseline predicts. This overlap persists for rejected draft tokens and reduces the unique expert count during SD verification (§ 6 ). • We show that activated-expert bytes are a poor proxy for runtime at batch size 1 on both H100 and B200, and use detailed GPU profiling to identify the H100 mechanisms, HBM-bandwidth utilization gaps between MoE and attention kernels and L2 cache reuse for small expert shards, and to show that these mechanisms are kernel-dependent (§ 7 ). • We introduce a maximum-entropy IPF framework that predicts unique expert counts within 4% error and generates realistic token-to-expert assignments. Sparse MoE architectures trace back to sparsely-gated MoE [ 44 ] and later scaling and routing designs such as GShard [ 30 ] , BASE Layers [ 32 ] , Switch Transformers [ 17 ] , GLaM [ 15 ] , and Expert Choice Routing [ 57 ] . More recent language-model variants increasingly use finer-grained and shared-expert designs [ 28 , 8 , 24 , 11 , 55 , 16 ] . Prior work [ 40 , 3 ] shows that expert co-activation is influenced by semantic and positional similarity, and ExpertFlow [ 20 ] exploits this locality for memory-constrained deployment. We build on this line of work by quantifying how temporal locality across consecutive draft tokens changes speculative-verification cost. Speculative decoding. Early work [ 47 ] introduced a prefix-validation approach for parallel autoregressive decoding. Modern speculative decoding methods differ mainly in how they construct and verify proposals: draft-model and seq2seq variants [ 31 , 5 , 53 ] , retrieval- or tree-based proposals [ 21 , 49 , 38 , 50 ] , extra decoding heads and multi-token prediction [ 4 , 2 , 19 , 11 , 55 ] , and higher-capacity or parallel drafting variants [ 35 , 34 , 36 , 18 , 25 , 22 ] . Recent work has shown that SD can remain effective outside the traditional small-batch dense regime, but for different reasons. MagicDec [ 42 ] shows that in long-context serving, large batches can again favor SD because KV-cache traffic dominates verification cost. The closest prior work for MoE is MoESD [ 23 ] , which models verification under an activated-expert-bytes view and accordingly predicts concave speedup curves with limited gains at low batch sizes. Because memory constraints typically force batch size down as sequence length grows, this low-batch regime is increasingly relevant for the longer-context, long-tailed RL rollout, and agentic workloads emerging in practice. Our work revisits this question for modern sparse MoEs and identifies a distinct regime in which fine-grained MoEs remain effective even at low batch sizes: temporal routing overlap and GPU execution dynamics yield higher speedup than the activated-expert-bytes view predicts. 3 Background and Experimental Setup Each SD iteration has two phases: (1) a draft model proposes K K tokens, and (2) the target model verifies these draft tokens together with the next-token continuation in a single pass over K + 1 K{+}1 positions. SD helps Time per output token (TPOT) only when the savings from fewer target-model calls exceed the overhead of verification—i.e., when acceptance is high and verification is cheap. In MoE models, this verification cost depends not only on model size but also on routing behavior, because verifying multiple tokens may activate overlapping sets of experts across the K + 1 K{+}1 positions. Because different SD mechanisms have different acceptance behavior, we isolate the target-side verification cost using target efficiency (TE) [ 23 ] , TE = T target AR / T target SD , \mathrm{TE}=T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{AR}}/T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{SD}}, where T target AR T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{AR}} denotes the latency of a single-token autoregressive (AR) decoding step on the target model and T target SD T_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{SD}} denotes the latency of the target model’s verification pass over K + 1 K{+}1 positions in speculative decoding (SD). A higher TE indicates that the SD verification pass is closer in cost to a standard AR decoding step. Because TE is independent of acceptance length, it lets us compare target-side verification efficiency across draft mechanisms and model architectures. The 10 evaluated MoE models span sparsity ratios (k/N, top-k over total experts) from 0.25 (Mixtral) to 0.020 (Qwen3-Next-80B), and per-expert weights from 4.7 MB to 176 MB in FP8, a 37× range that proves critical for GPU execution dynamics (§ 5 ); Appendix Table 6 lists the full architectural details and SD methods. Section 6 and Section 7 show that both temporal overlap and GPU execution dynamics shape the SD speedup curves of MoE models. We therefore conduct synthetic experiments that combine these two factors to predict the speedup curves without using trained weights. The only assumption is access to reasonable expert-overlap statistics, obtained either from a model in the same family or from the averages in Table 17 . To evaluate the IPF framework from Section 6.3 and its synthetic-routing construction from Appendix L , we replace the model’s learned routing with IPF-generated synthetic routing while keeping all other inference settings fixed (dummy weights, same hardware). Because this method runs the real kernels on the target hardware, it captures hardware- and kernel-specific execution effects, such as those that differ between H100 and B200, without modeling them explicitly. We define the proxy target efficiency as T vanilla proxy / T SD proxy T_{\text{vanilla}}^{\text{proxy}}/T_{\text{SD}}^{\text{proxy}} , where T vanilla proxy T_{\text{vanilla}}^{\text{proxy}} = forward pass + logits + sampling, and T SD proxy T_{\text{SD}}^{\text{proxy}} = forward pass + logits + rejection sampling + draft. We measure the proxy target efficiency under three routing assumptions: uniform random routing, uniform IPF routing with the same routing-overlap statistics in every MoE layer, and per-layer skewed IPF routing. Figure 2 compares these three settings. The uniform-random baseline consistently underestimates the target efficiency at small batch sizes, and the error is larger for sparser MoE models. Per-layer IPF synthetic routing closely tracks the real-model curves at small batch sizes and remains closer than uniform random routing across the full batch-size range. Long context thus makes verification relatively cheaper for the MoE target; MagicDec [ 42 ] studies this regime in depth. 9.3 Implications for MoE Draft Layers Current SD drafters commonly use a dense transformer layer. In Appendix M , we use the framework from Section 8 to analyze the effect of an MoE drafter when the target model is also an MoE model. The analysis suggests that MoE draft layers may become attractive in sufficiently sparse regimes. At low-to-medium batch sizes, an MoE drafter does not improve target efficiency, but if trained effectively it could still improve end-to-end speedup through longer acceptance lengths enabled by its additional parameters. At larger batch sizes, the MoE drafter becomes more attractive because it remains less compute-bound than a dense drafter when the target model itself is MoE. To probe a sparser setting than Qwen3-30B, we also simulate a 896-expert architecture (<1% activations) and show in Appendix M.3 that the MoE drafter becomes more favorable as the target model remains bandwidth-bound. Because this analysis is synthetic and does not measure acceptance-length gains from trained MoE drafters, we interpret it as a design study rather than direct evidence for trained MoE drafters. 9.4 Routing Inertia in Rejected Draft Tokens Expert routing does not cleanly separate accepted from rejected draft tokens in a way that would support early termination. In the aggregate MT-Bench analysis, fine-grained models show comparable or slightly higher overlap for rejected tokens, and held-out Spec-Bench and Aya [ 45 ] slices preserve the same tendency in median, with some task- and language-specific reversals (Appendix H.8 ). Even in the largest stable aggregate effect (Qwen3-235B, Cohen’s d ≈ − 0.3 d\approx-0.3 ), the accepted and rejected distributions still overlap by ∼ 85 % {\sim}85\% , and most held-out slices remain negligible or small in effect size. These results suggest that routing-based rejection predictors are unlikely to be useful in practice: routing inertia is statistically robust but offers limited leverage for early-exit decisions. 10 Conclusion As sparse MoE models move into increasingly memory-constrained inference regimes, an important question is whether speculative decoding remains worthwhile at low batch size. Across 10 recent sparse MoE models (30B–1T parameters, 8–512 experts), we find that the previously expected concave SD speedup curve does not characterize most modern sparse models: many attain high speedup at or near batch size 1. We show that verification cost in sparse MoE models is not determined by activated-expert bytes alone, but is also shaped by temporal overlap across consecutive tokens and by GPU execution dynamics, whose specific mechanisms vary across hardware and kernels. A maximum-entropy IPF framework predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4% error and, under synthetic routing with fixed execution conditions, substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves while capturing the qualitative low-batch trend, thereby providing a train-free way to study target and draft architecture tradeoffs. Taken together, these results suggest that SD performance on sparse MoE models should be modeled using both routing-overlap statistics and GPU execution dynamics, and that fine-grained MoE designs may be more compatible with low-batch speculative inference than previously believed.
